title: SEC Probes Nvidia’s Disclosures After Jensen Huang’s Departure
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia following the resignation of Chief Executive Jensen Huang, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The civil inquiry includes whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors. The full scope of the investigation remains unclear, and the SEC declined to comment. Nvidia did not respond to Bloomberg’s request for comment on the report.

Nvidia announced on Nov. 12 that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. The board appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. She will retain her finance duties while the board considers internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.

The Journal reported that investors have raised questions about Nvidia’s disclosures concerning Huang’s relationships and the company’s chip sales in Asia. Nvidia previously denied that Huang had an unusual relationship with Alice Huang, then an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. The Journal also reported that Nvidia changed how it presented international sales last year and stopped separately disclosing sales to Singapore.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced a separate inquiry Thursday and said his office had served Nvidia with an investigative subpoena. State investigators are examining whether advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether Nvidia misled investors or the public about that risk. The subpoena seeks information to help determine whether the company violated California law.

The scrutiny comes as Nvidia’s data-center business continues to expand. The company reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data-center segment. Nvidia said it would file its full quarterly report in the coming weeks. That filing typically includes updates on risk factors, legal proceedings and internal controls over financial reporting.
